extracted.intended_audience: humor scholars, folklorists, linguists, and researchers in humor studies
extracted.subtask_description: An academic book review of Elliott Oring's The Consolations of Humor and Other Folklore Essays, summarizing and assessing theoretical positions about humor, script theory, context, and folklore methodology. Useful for researchers evaluating theoretical criteria for analyzing humorous texts and folklore.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate incongruity
rubrics_metrics.description: Oring defends the notion of 'appropriate incongruity' as central to humor theory (an incongruity must be appropriate to the context for humor to arise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oring contrasts appropriate incongruity with other formulations (e.g., Raskin's script opposition). The reviewer notes that appropriateness is contextual/local (an opposition may be 'only opposed in the world of the joke'). Example discussion: one-liners about 'man of letters' illustrate distinctions between global and local opposition. Anti-pattern: treating incongruity as context-free.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spurious incongruity / paralogicality
rubrics_metrics.description: Oring emphasizes that incongruity must be not only appropriate but also 'spurious'—i.e., marked, manipulative, oversimplifying or prioritizing one script over another (translated in terms of paralogicality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book argues that spuriousness is what makes an incongruity humorous; translators and analysts should note that 'spurious' can be hard to render in some languages. Example: Oring's claim that the appropriateness of 'the man of letters who produces nothing of literary value' is not spurious and thus produces no humor. Avoid analyses that do not account for spurious/marked quality of the incongruity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Script opposition (SSTH) and its contextual/local character
rubrics_metrics.description: Script opposition (Raskin's move to replace 'incongruity' with 'opposition') is necessarily contextual; many oppositions are local rather than global.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts should treat script oppositions as context-dependent—determine whether an opposition is invoked by the language of the joke alone or by broader context/knowledge. Example: difference between one-liners where 'man of letters' evokes writer vs postman scripts. Warning against assuming opposition is always global.

rubrics_metrics.name: Script overlap: insufficient definition and limited applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Oring criticizes the SSTH notion of 'overlap' of scripts as insufficiently defined and not universally exemplified by many supposed cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t assume 'overlap' merely when an element of one script appears in another; the DOCTOR/LOVER model is a specific kind of overlap and not all cases fit. Oring treats some alleged overlaps (e.g., Great Barzini joke) as misanalyses. Analysts should be explicit about what constitutes overlap and consider connector/disjunctor proposals (Attardo) where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical mechanism (GTVH) should not be overgeneralized
rubrics_metrics.description: Oring criticizes the 'logical mechanism' concept (used in later script theory/GTVH) as too powerful and insufficiently specific to humor because it appears in non-humorous texts as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using logical-mechanism explanations, assess whether the mechanism uniquely accounts for humor or whether it is a general interpretive device found in non-humorous discourse; avoid attributing humor solely to broad logical mechanisms without demonstrating specificity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual factors in interpretation (Hymes' 'Speaking' model)
rubrics_metrics.description: To interpret humorous/folkloric texts one must consider context: 'who said what to whom in what situation, through which medium and with what intention' (Hymes). Oring stresses the role of the nature of the joke, the character of the teller, the person to whom it is told and the circumstances of the telling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should include teller/recipient/setting/medium/intention. Example: discussion of humor scandals (army officer sexual jokes) demonstrates the importance of situational context. Anti-pattern: analyzing jokes only as textual objects without situational grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text (sense) vs texture (linguistic formulation): form is meaningful
rubrics_metrics.description: Oring follows Dundes' distinction between text ('sense') and texture ('linguistic formulation'), arguing they are 'not actually separate... but nonetheless can be distinguished' and that form (e.g., rhyme) is part of meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars should treat linguistic form (rhythm, rhyme, phrasing) as carrying sense; beware of analyses that sever form and content. Example: 'Red sky at morning, sailors take warning' — rhyme contributes to sense and may be lost in translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content factors that promote replicability and memorability
rubrics_metrics.description: Oring lists content features that help stories/jokes be replicated and memorable: the mysterious, the counterintuitive, the morally positive, the fear-inducing and salacious, the amusing, or content that promotes sociability and survival.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating why a story/joke spreads, consider these content dimensions. The reviewer notes individual creativity is also cited but treated as an unsatisfying ultimate explanation. Empirical work should test which content factors correlate with transmission and memorability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely solely on 'creativity'—seek rules/laws and avoid tautologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Oring calls for folklorists to search for rules and laws that explain reproduction and survival of folklore items rather than appealing only to creativity; he warns against tautologies, flawed definitions and wrong interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research should attempt explicit, testable principles about tradition and memetics, and explicitly avoid circular explanations (e.g., 'it spread because it was good') or vague appeals to genius. Methodological note: clarify concepts and operationalize variables to prevent tautological reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptualizing humor as primarily intellectual (not aggression-based)
rubrics_metrics.description: Oring advances the idea that humor is mainly an intellectual process—a philosophy of sorts—that evokes emotions only secondarily and is not explainable by aggression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts should foreground cognitive/intellectual mechanisms (knowledge, inference, perspective shifts) in accounts of humor rather than defaulting to aggression-based explanations. Empirical tests should separate cognitive/inferential causes from affective/aggressive interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dirty/sexual jokes: study as amusement (not arousal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Oring argues that dirty jokes are really meant to amuse, not to arouse, and should be revived as a subject of scholarly study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat sexual/dirty jokes first as humor objects with social/interactional functions. Avoid reductive readings that privilege erotic intent; document contexts of telling and reception to assess pragmatic function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of character knowledge and character frames
rubrics_metrics.description: Access to context and knowledge of characters (character frames) is necessary for humor to appear; perspective shifts and knowledge about characters help make incongruities appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include character frames in analyses—what the audience knows about characters and perspectives often determines which script oppositions or incongruities are salient. Example: AI-generated joke showing humor arises by attributing unexpected thoughts/knowledge to characters (man vs dog).
